context_blurb:
Right now, as you read, your heart is beating and your lungs are filling with air. These are organs: body parts that each do one main job. Working together, they keep you alive, and you can feel some of them at work if you know where to look.

Lay two fingertips on the inside of your wrist, just below your thumb, and you will feel a steady throb. That throb is your pulse, and each one comes from a single beat of your heart. The heart is a muscle about the size of a fist, and with each beat it squeezes and pumps blood around the body. The throb in your wrist is that push of blood arriving. Count the throbs for one minute: for most children your age, the number lands between 70 and 110. The heart does not make blood, though. New blood is made in the soft marrow inside your bones.

Blood travels through a huge network of tubes that reaches every part of you. Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and digested food in the small intestine, and it brings both to every part of the body. On the way back, it carries wastes away.

One waste comes from your cells themselves. When cells use oxygen to break down food for energy, a waste gas called carbon dioxide is left over. The blood brings it back to the lungs. There, through the thin walls of tiny air sacs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood, while carbon dioxide passes out the other way, and you breathe it out. Carbon dioxide is not the same as carbon monoxide, a poison gas given off when fuel burns badly in stoves and engines.

Each swallowed mouthful travels down the food pipe to the stomach, a stretchy bag of muscle that can swell to hold a meal. Inside the stomach, strong acid juices soak the food while the muscular walls squeeze and mix it, until it turns into a thick, soupy mush.

Next the mush moves on to the small intestine, a narrow tube that lies coiled in loops in the belly. It is called small because it is narrow, not because it is short. Its lining is covered in tiny finger-like bumps called villi. Most of the digested food passes through the villi into the blood, which carries it all over the body. What is left moves on to the large intestine, which takes out water and forms solid waste.

Your brain is in charge of the whole body, and it needs a way to send orders and get news. Nerves are thread-like bundles that branch out from the brain and spinal cord to every part of the body, carrying messages both ways. Some nerves bring news in from your eyes, ears and skin. Others carry the brain's orders out to your muscles.

Bones give the body its frame. An adult has about 206 of them, and together they hold you upright and give your body its shape, the way poles hold up a tent. Some bones also guard soft organs. The skull, made of 22 bones joined together, forms a hard case around the brain. Your ribs make a cage around your heart and lungs.

Muscles move bones by pulling on them. The biceps sits on the front of your upper arm. When the biceps works, it gets shorter and pulls the forearm up through a tough cord called a tendon, so the elbow bends. A muscle can pull, but it can never push. So muscles work in pairs: to straighten the elbow again, the triceps on the back of the arm does the pulling. Grip your upper arm and bend your elbow, and you can feel your biceps at work.

Which organ is the biggest? Most people never think of the skin as an organ, but it is one. The skin is the largest organ of all: an adult's skin weighs nearly 4 kilograms, more than twice as much as the biggest organ inside the body. It wraps the whole body, keeps germs out and water in, and lets you feel heat, cold and touch.
